subtopic: Building insurance and an emergency fund
subtype: Approach: rule for what counts as emergency [Action]
passage:
Sit, Lalremsiami. You asked how I keep my savings when everyone around me is tempted. I'm Pranav, and I'll tell you about a small card.
Years ago I built a cushion, and then a sale came, then a friend planned a trip, and each time the cushion looked like free money. So one night I wrote on a card: "Only for a hospital bill, losing my job, or a leaking roof. Nothing else."
It sat in my wallet. When my friend Ranjit called about the trip, I took the card out and read it. A trip was none of those three. I said no, and he laughed.
Months later, the roof did leak, and I opened the fund without a second thought.

qa.q: What three things did the card list?
qa.a: The card listed a hospital bill, losing a job, and a leaking roof.

qa.q: What was Pranav probably feeling during the sale and the trip invitation?
qa.a: Pranav was tempted, since the cushion looked like free money, but the card steadied that pull.

qa.q: Pranav wrote a short rule on a card. What did that choice help with?
qa.a: It settled in advance what counted as an emergency, so a sale or a trip could not talk Pranav into using the cushion.

qa.q: How might Ranjit have felt when Pranav said no to the trip?
qa.a: Ranjit took it lightly and laughed, so was probably a little disappointed but not offended.

grounding: The elder's story shows a person writing a short if-then rule about which emergencies allow a withdrawal so that sales and trips do not drain the fund.

passage:
Arohi's voice note came in at 9 p.m.: 'Group booking closes at midnight! Fourteen thousand each, Goa, you in?' Swati was already on her balcony with a notebook, because the same thing had nearly happened in April with a sofa sale.
She wrote it slowly, like a rule for a board game:
IF a hospital bill, OR I lose my job, OR the flat needs a repair that can't wait, THEN I can touch the fund.
IF it is a sale, a trip, a gift or a gadget, THEN it comes from the monthly spend account, or it waits.
She clipped the page inside her wardrobe door, next to the fund's account number. Then she checked the monthly spend account: six thousand. Not enough.
At 11.40 she replied to Arohi: 'Can't this time 😔 Send photos? Next trip I'm saving for properly.'

qa.q: How much was in Swati's monthly spend account?
qa.a: Six thousand, which was not enough for the trip.

qa.q: What was Swati feeling when she replied at 11.40?
qa.a: Swati felt disappointed to miss the trip 😔 but also steady, because the rule she had just written made the choice clear.

qa.q: What other approach could help Swati join trips without touching the fund?
qa.a: She could keep a separate small pot for trips and add to it through the year, so the next invitation has its own money.

qa.q: How might Arohi read Swati's reply?
qa.a: Arohi might be disappointed that the group is one short, but the promise about the next trip shows that Swati still wants to come.

grounding: It shows a young woman writing an if-then rule that allows fund withdrawals only for medical bills, job loss or urgent repairs, so a trip cannot drain it.

passage:
Naveen stuck a yellow note inside his cupboard in their Chennai flat, just above the file where the fund's passbook lived. It said, in capitals: WITHDRAW ONLY IF 1. hospital, 2. job gone, 3. urgent repair to the flat. NOT for sales, trips, weddings.
'Weddings?' his wife, Trisha, asked, reading over his shoulder.
'Last year my cousin's wedding took half of it,' he said. 'Never again.'
Two weeks later a big thin TV was on offer, and Naveen caught himself opening the passbook. He read the note, closed the file and saved the TV to a wish list instead.
In October the bathroom pipe burst and water crept under the bedroom door. The plumber quoted nine thousand. This time Naveen opened the file without any guilt, and Trisha said, 'See? That's what it's for.'

qa.q: What was Naveen feeling when he opened the file in October?
qa.a: He felt calm and free of guilt, because the burst pipe clearly matched his rule for an urgent repair.

qa.q: What small step could make Naveen's rule even stronger?
qa.a: He and Trisha could agree the rule together and decide how to handle grey cases, so both of them apply it the same way.

qa.q: How does the note look to Trisha?
qa.a: At first she questions why weddings are banned, but when the pipe bursts she sees the rule working and backs it.

grounding: It shows a young man writing a short rule that lets the fund be used only for hospital, job loss or urgent repair, and then keeping to it.
